name: Peruvian Ceviche
why: Citrus-cured fish is the perfect palate reset after a week of stews and bakes - a new technique (the lemon "cooks" the fish raw) and a 20-minute dish that tastes like it took all afternoon. Peak summer: bright, cold, and gone in minutes.
author: Henry
ingredients: 400g skinless sea bass, lemon sole or snapper fillets, pin-boned, from sustainable sources

steps: Deseed and very finely chop the pepper; trim and finely slice the spring onions. Add both to a bowl.
Slice the fish into neat 1cm cubes, add to the bowl, then cover and chill in the fridge until just before serving.
Squeeze the juice of all 3 lemons into a jam jar, add 1 tsp sea salt, then seed, finely chop and add the chilli. Cover and chill. (It looks like a lot of salt, but most gets drained away.)
Pick the mint, coriander and mustard cress, keeping a few sprigs back for garnish. Chill.
Assemble only when you are ready to serve - never let the fish sit in the dressing for long, or the acid will overcook it.
Pour the lemon dressing over the fish and pepper mixture and mix immediately.
Leave to sit for about 2-3 minutes while you lay out the plates and set the table.
Toss most of the picked herbs through the ceviche - a fast 10-second toss, no longer.
Divide between 4 plates, spoon over a little dressing (discard the rest) and scatter over the remaining herbs.
Drizzle with good olive oil from a height, grind over black pepper, and serve at once.

pro_tips: The clock starts the moment the lemon hits the fish - 2-3 minutes gives that translucent, seared edge while the centres stay silky. Over 10 minutes and it turns mealy.

Jamie uses fresh mint and cress instead of the classic cilantro-heavy Peruvian mix - it tastes much lighter. For a more traditional take, swap half the mint for extra coriander and add diced red onion and sweet potato for the full Lima experience.
